blogs.title: 7 Signs Your Home Might Have a Hidden Water Leak
blogs.shortDescription: Small leaks can become expensive problems. Learn the warning signs that could indicate a hidden plumbing leak.
blogs.summary: The leaks that cause real damage are almost never the dramatic ones. They are slow, hidden behind a wall or under a floor, and they run for weeks before anything shows. These are the signs worth acting on, and the simple test that will tell you for certain whether you have one.

children.text: 1. Running water in a quiet house

Stand in the hallway late at night with everything switched off and listen. A faint hiss or trickle with no tap open is one of the most reliable indicators there is, and it often appears months before any visible damage. Put an ear to the wall in a few places and the sound usually gets louder near the source.
2. A patch of lawn greener than the rest

If the supply line runs under the garden, a leak feeds the grass above it. A strip or patch that stays lush in dry weather, or ground that feels soft underfoot when it has not rained, is pointing directly at the pipe beneath.
3. Tap water that tastes or smells different

A leak on a buried supply line can draw soil and bacteria in through the same opening water escapes from, particularly when pressure drops. A sudden earthy or metallic taste from a tap that was fine last week deserves checking rather than filtering.
4. Paint or wallpaper that bubbles

Moisture arriving from behind lifts a decorated surface away from the wall before it ever stains it. Blistering paint, a seam of wallpaper peeling on its own, or a bulge in plasterboard all mean water is already in the structure.
5. Mould that keeps returning to the same spot

Mould cleaned off a wall and back within a fortnight is not a ventilation problem. Something is keeping that area permanently damp, and in a bathroom or kitchen it is very often a joint behind the tiling rather than condensation.
6. The pump or boiler cycling more often

A system that loses pressure continuously has to work harder to hold it. If your boiler needs topping up more frequently than it used to, or a pressure pump is starting several times an hour with nothing running, water is going somewhere.
“By the time a hidden leak is visible, it has usually been running long enough to have done the expensive part of the damage already.”
7. Confirm it with the meter test

Turn off every tap and appliance in the house, including the ice maker and any irrigation. Note the exact meter reading, wait two hours without using water, and read it again. Any movement means an active leak somewhere on your side of the meter.

That test costs nothing and rules the question in or out completely. If it moves, book a leak detection visit rather than opening walls — acoustic and thermal equipment will find the spot in under an hour without taking anything apart.

seo.metaTitle: 7 Signs Your Home Might Have a Hidden Water Leak

blogs.title: How to Keep Your Drains Clear and Flowing
blogs.shortDescription: Simple habits that stop slow drains and blockages before they turn into an emergency call-out.
blogs.summary: Most blocked drains are not bad luck. They are the result of a few months of small habits, and they give plenty of warning before they finally stop draining altogether. Keeping them clear is mostly about what never goes down them in the first place, plus a handful of minutes each month.

children.text: 1. Keep fats and oils out of the sink entirely

Cooking fat pours as a liquid and sets as a solid somewhere down the line where it is cold. It then catches everything else that passes. Pour it into a jar, let it set, and put it in the bin — this one habit prevents more kitchen blockages than anything else on this list.
2. Strainers beat drain cleaner every time

A few pounds of mesh strainer in each sink, basin and shower catches hair, food and grit before it enters the pipe at all. Emptying one takes two seconds. It is considerably cheaper and considerably kinder to your pipework than any bottled product.
3. Hot water alone is not a flush

Running the hot tap for a few seconds moves grease further along the pipe rather than removing it. A proper monthly flush is a full kettle of very hot water poured steadily down the kitchen drain, ideally last thing at night when nothing else will be used.

If you want to add something, a handful of bicarbonate followed by vinegar and then the hot water is fine. Avoid caustic drain cleaners as routine maintenance — they damage older pipe and seals, and they do nothing a flush does not.
4. Give the bathroom drains a weekly minute

Shower and basin drains block with hair and soap scum, not grease, so they need a different habit. Lift the grate, pull out what has gathered, and run the tap hot for thirty seconds. Doing it weekly takes a minute; doing it never takes a plumber.
“A drain that has started running slow is not yet a problem. It is the only warning you are going to get before it becomes one.”
5. Listen to what a slow drain is telling you

One slow fixture is a local clog and usually clears with a plunger or a hand auger. Several slow at once means the shared line downstream is restricting, and that is a different job entirely — no amount of work at the plughole will reach it.

Gurgling from a nearby drain when you empty a sink is worth attention too. It usually means air is being pulled through a trap because the line is partly blocked, and it tends to appear well before anything stops draining.

blogs.title: How to Know When to Fix or Swap Out Your Water Heater
blogs.shortDescription: Rising bills, rusty water and uneven heat all hint at whether a repair or a replacement is the smarter spend.
blogs.summary: A water heater rarely fails without warning. It gets noisier, it runs out of hot water sooner, the water looks slightly off, and the bill creeps up. The question is whether those symptoms add up to a repair worth paying for or a unit that is quietly telling you its remaining life is short.

children.text: 1. Start with the age of the unit

A conventional tank heater runs about eight to twelve years; a tankless unit often reaches twenty. Find the serial number on the data plate — most manufacturers encode the build date in the first four characters. Everything else you decide follows from that number, because a repair on a two-year-old unit and the same repair on an eleven-year-old unit are completely different propositions.
2. Rusty water points at the tank itself

Discoloured hot water that runs clear on the cold side means corrosion inside the tank rather than in the supply. Sometimes that is a spent sacrificial anode, which is a genuine repair. Often it is the glass lining having failed, which is not repairable at any price.
3. Weigh the repair against the remaining life

A thermostat, a heating element or a pressure relief valve is a modest bill and worth doing on almost any unit that is not already past its expected life. A failed tank, a cracked heat exchanger or a gas valve on an older unit is usually a large enough share of replacement cost that you are paying twice.
The rough rule most plumbers use is simple: if the repair costs more than half a new unit and the heater is past two thirds of its expected life, replace it.
4. Efficiency belongs in the sum

A heater from a decade ago is meaningfully less efficient than a current one, and in a household using hot water daily that difference shows up on every bill for the next ten years. It does not justify replacing a healthy unit, but it does tilt a borderline decision.
“The most expensive water heater is the one you repair three times in its last two years and then replace anyway.”
5. A leaking tank ends the conversation

Water pooling under the unit from a fitting is a repair. Water seeping from the body of the tank is not — that is the tank wall itself, and there is no fix for it. Once a tank starts weeping it should be replaced promptly, because they tend to fail properly rather than politely.

If you find standing water under the heater, shut off the supply and the power or gas to the unit before anything else, then call someone. A tank that lets go holds a lot more water than most people expect.

blogs.title: Why Your Water Pressure Drops, and What Fixes It
blogs.shortDescription: From a half-closed stopcock to a failing valve, where pressure really goes
blogs.summary: Weak pressure is rarely the mains; it is usually one valve, one filter or one corroded run

children.text: 1. The stopcock is not fully open

This is the first thing to rule out and the cheapest to fix. An internal stopcock that was closed for a repair and only turned back most of the way will throttle the whole house. Open it fully, then back it off a quarter turn so it does not seize in place.
2. A blocked aerator on one tap

If the problem is at a single outlet rather than across the house, unscrew the aerator at the tip of the spout. Grit and scale collect in that mesh and choke the flow. Soak it overnight in descaler, rinse it and refit it before assuming anything larger is wrong.
3. Limescale narrowing the pipework

In a hard water area the internal diameter of a pipe shrinks year by year as scale builds. It happens slowly enough that nobody notices until a shower feels weak, and it affects the hot side first because heat accelerates the deposit.
4. A failing pressure-reducing valve

Most homes have a valve that holds incoming pressure at a safe level. When its internal diaphragm perishes it tends to fail low, and the drop arrives across every outlet at once rather than gradually. Replacing it is a short job with an immediate result.
5. A leak between the main and the house

Water escaping on the supply side never reaches your taps, so pressure falls and the bill rises together. If the meter creeps with everything closed, the loss is underground and needs tracing before anything indoors is touched.
6. Too many outlets on one run

Pressure that collapses the moment a second tap opens is usually a sizing problem rather than a fault. An undersized run feeding a whole bathroom simply cannot supply two fixtures at once, and resizing that section solves it permanently.
“Almost every weak shower we are called to turns out to be one restricted component, not a whole house that needs repiping.”
7. A problem at the mains, not in your home

Occasionally nothing indoors is wrong. Street works, a supplier valve left part-closed, or peak demand on a shared run will all show up as poor pressure. A gauge on the outside tap tells us in minutes which side of the boundary the fault sits on.
Any one of these can account for a weak shower. Two together usually explain a whole house that has quietly lost its pressure over a year or two.

blogs.title: Five Signs You Need a Plumber, Not a YouTube Video
blogs.shortDescription: Some jobs really are a ten minute fix. These five are the ones where a tutorial costs more than a call-out.
blogs.summary: Plenty of plumbing really is a ten minute job with a spanner and a tutorial. Swapping a washer, clearing a trap, replacing a toilet flapper — all fair game. The problem is that the jobs which look similar from the outside are not similar at all, and a few of them turn a small bill into a very large one the moment you start.

children.text: 1. The shut-off valve will not close fully

Before any repair, the first test is whether you can actually stop the water. If the isolation valve is seized, weeping or only closes halfway, every job downstream of it becomes a job you cannot undo. That is the point to stop, because the valve itself is now the repair and it needs the mains off to change.
2. You cannot tell where the water is coming from

Water travels along joists, under boards and down the outside of pipes before it appears. A damp patch on a ceiling is rarely directly under its source. If you cannot trace it to a fitting you can see and touch, opening up the nearest surface is guesswork — and usually the wrong surface.
3. The fix involves a joint you will never see again

A compression fitting under a sink can be redone in a minute if it weeps. The same fitting buried in a wall cannot. Any joint that is about to be covered by tile, plaster or screed needs to be made by someone whose work you can hold to account, because testing it properly is a skill in itself.
The cost of getting that one joint wrong is not the joint. It is the tiling, the plastering and the drying-out afterwards.
4. It is a gas appliance

Anything connected to a gas supply — a combi boiler, a gas water heater, a gas hob being moved for a new sink — is not a DIY job in any circumstance, regardless of how straightforward the plumbing side looks. It is also, in most places, illegal to work on without certification.
“The question is never whether you can do the repair. It is what happens if it fails at three in the morning while you are asleep upstairs.”
5. You have already fixed it twice

A repair that needs doing again within a few months was never the real fix. The tap that keeps dripping after two new washers has a damaged seat. The drain that blocks every spring has something structural going on further down the line.

At that point a third attempt costs more than a diagnosis. Someone with a camera and a pressure gauge will find the actual cause in an hour, and you will have spent less than you did on the parts for attempts one and two.

blogs.title: Preparing Your Pipes Before the First Freeze
blogs.shortDescription: An hour of lagging and draining in autumn is the cheapest insurance against a burst pipe in January.
blogs.summary: Nothing about a frozen pipe is gradual. It holds, and holds, and then it splits — usually overnight, usually in the part of the house nobody visits in winter. An hour of work in autumn is the cheapest insurance available against a January morning spent moving furniture out of a flooded room.

children.text: 1. Find the pipes that sit in unheated space

Lofts, garages, crawl spaces, the run behind an external wall and anything under a suspended floor are where pipes freeze first. Walk the house once with a torch before the weather turns and note every length of pipe that is not surrounded by heated air. Those are the ones that need attention; the rest largely look after themselves.
2. Drain and disconnect the outside taps

Detach every hose, open the outside tap fully, then close the indoor isolation valve that feeds it and leave the outside tap open over winter. Water trapped between a closed valve and a connected hose has nowhere to expand, and an outside tap is the single most common place a freeze does its damage.
3. Lagging only works where it actually covers

Foam sleeve insulation is inexpensive and effective, but it protects exactly the length of pipe it wraps and nothing more. The gaps people leave — at bends, at valves, where the pipe passes through a joist — are precisely the spots that freeze, because that is where the metal is most exposed.
Cut the sleeves to fit the bends rather than leaving them short, and tape the seams. A continuous run of cheap lagging beats an expensive product fitted with gaps in it.
4. Let a tap trickle on the coldest nights

On the handful of nights each winter when the temperature really drops, open the tap furthest from the stopcock just enough for a steady drip. Moving water is far harder to freeze than still water, and the trickle also relieves the pressure that actually splits the pipe when ice does form.
“A pipe rarely bursts at the spot where it froze. It bursts between the ice and the closed tap, where the pressure has nowhere left to go.”
5. Know where your stop tap is before you need it

Find the main shut-off now, check it turns, and make sure everyone in the house knows where it is. A seized stopcock discovered during a burst is a much worse problem than a seized stopcock discovered in October.

If you are going away over winter, either leave the heating on a low setting or drain the system down properly. An empty house at four degrees for a fortnight is how most serious freeze damage happens.

blogs.title: Why Your Drain Is Slow: When Jetting Beats Snaking
blogs.shortDescription: A snake punches a hole through a blockage. Jetting scours the pipe wall. Here is when each one is the right call.
blogs.summary: A slow drain has two common cures and they are not interchangeable. A snake punches a hole through whatever is blocking the pipe so water can pass again. Jetting scours the pipe wall back to bare material. Choosing the wrong one means either paying too much for a simple clog or clearing the same blockage every few months.

children.text: 1. What a snake actually does

A drain snake is a flexible cable that is fed down the line until it reaches the obstruction, then rotated to break through it or hook it out. It is quick, inexpensive and ideal for a single fixture blocked by hair, a wipe or a build-up of soap. What it does not do is remove the material coating the pipe around the hole it just made.
2. What jetting does differently

Hydro jetting sends water down the line at high pressure through a nozzle that sprays backwards as well as forwards. That scours grease, scale and sludge off the pipe wall and flushes it away, leaving the full original diameter rather than a channel through the middle of the blockage.
3. Grease, roots and scale each need a different answer

Kitchen lines clogged with cooled fat are the clearest case for jetting — a snake will pass straight through soft grease and leave the walls exactly as coated as they were. Root intrusion usually needs a cutting head first and jetting afterwards to clear the debris.
A single bathroom drain blocked by hair, on the other hand, rarely justifies bringing a jetter to the property at all. Thirty seconds with a snake solves it.
4. When jetting is the wrong call

Old clay, cast iron that has corroded thin, or any line with a known crack should be inspected before jetting. The pressure that scours a sound pipe clean can open a weak one up. A plumber who jets an unknown line without looking first is taking a risk with your floor.
“If the same drain blocks twice in a year, the first clearance did not fail — it was the wrong method for what is actually in the pipe.”
5. Ask for a camera before you choose either one

A camera survey takes a few minutes and settles the question completely. It shows whether you are looking at a soft blockage, a hard scale layer, roots, a collapsed section or a fall that was laid wrong in the first place.
That last one matters most, because no amount of snaking or jetting fixes a pipe that does not drain downhill. Knowing which problem you have before paying for a cure is the whole point.

blogs.title: What to Plan For When Repiping a Kitchen Remodel
blogs.shortDescription: Repiping is far cheaper while the walls are already open. What to decide before the plasterboard goes back on.
blogs.summary: A kitchen remodel is the cheapest opportunity you will ever get to replace the pipework behind it. The walls are already open, the floor is already up, and the work that would normally cost a fortune in access is suddenly almost free. The decisions that matter all have to be made before the plasterboard goes back on.

children.text: 1. Decide the pipe material before demolition starts

Copper, PEX and CPVC all behave differently in a kitchen wall, and the choice affects routing, insulation and how the joints are made. Settling it early avoids the mid-job compromise where half the run is one material and half is another, joined by fittings nobody will be able to inspect later.
2. Map every fixture you might add later

A pot filler over the hob, a second sink in an island, a filtered tap, an ice maker in the fridge recess — each one needs a supply line. Roughing them in while the wall is open costs a fraction of what it costs to add one afterwards, even if you do not fit the fixture for another two years.
3. Shut-off valves are cheap now and expensive later

Every fixture should get its own isolation valve, positioned somewhere you can actually reach it without emptying a cupboard. It adds very little to the bill during a repipe and it means a future leak affects one tap rather than the whole house.
The same applies to the branch feeding the kitchen as a whole. One accessible valve on that line turns a future repair from a whole-day job with the mains off into an afternoon.
4. Sequence the trades so nothing gets buried

Plumbing goes in before electrics where the two compete for the same joist space, and both go in before insulation and boarding. Getting that order wrong is how supply lines end up notched through structural timber or run somewhere the inspector will not sign off.
“The expensive part of a repipe is never the pipe. It is the plaster, the tiling and the cabinetry you have to take apart to reach it — which is why doing it during a remodel is such good value.”
5. Budget for the inspection, not just the materials

Most areas require a rough-in inspection before anything is covered up, and a final inspection once the fixtures are connected. Both take time to schedule, and a failed rough-in means the boarding waits.
Build that into the programme from the start. A week of slack in the schedule costs nothing; discovering you need it after the plasterer is booked costs a great deal.

blogs.title: Is a Plumbing Contract Worth It?
blogs.shortDescription: What an annual plan actually covers, what it does not, and the number of call-outs where it starts paying for itself.
blogs.summary: An annual plumbing contract is the sort of thing you sign once and then forget about, which is exactly the point for some households and exactly the problem for others. Whether it earns its keep comes down to the age of your pipework, how many fixtures you have, and how often you have already had to call someone out at short notice.

children.text: 1. What an annual plan actually includes

Most plans cover one scheduled inspection a year, a water heater flush, a check of every shut-off valve and visible joint, and a discount on labour for anything found during the visit. The inspection is the part that matters — it is where small problems get caught while they are still cheap to fix.
2. What it almost never covers

Replacement parts, fixtures and appliances are nearly always billed separately. So is anything behind a wall or under a slab that needs excavation. A plan lowers the cost of getting someone there and diagnosing the problem; it does not turn a failed water heater into a free water heater.
3. The break-even point is lower than most people expect

A plan tends to cover its own cost somewhere around the second call-out of the year, once the waived emergency fee and the labour discount are counted together. If you called a plumber twice last year, the maths already works in your favour.

If you called nobody at all last year and your plumbing is under ten years old, the plan is buying you an inspection you could book on its own for less. That is a fair trade for some people and a waste for others.
4. Priority booking is the real benefit

The part people underrate is where you sit in the queue. On the first freezing weekend of the year, every plumber in the area is booked solid. Contract customers get slotted in first, and on a burst pipe that difference is measured in ruined flooring rather than pounds.
“Almost nobody reads the exclusions until the day they need them. Ten minutes with the terms before you sign is worth more than the discount on the front of the leaflet.”
5. When you are better off without one

New-build homes with modern pipework and a warranty still running rarely need a plan in the first few years. The same goes for a flat with a single bathroom and a combi boiler that the building already services.
Where a plan earns its money is an older property, a house with two or more bathrooms, or anywhere you cannot afford to be without hot water for three days while you wait for an appointment.

blogs.title: How Long Should a Water Heater Actually Last?
blogs.shortDescription: Tank, tankless and hard water all change the answer. What to expect and the signs yours is near the end.
blogs.summary: A dripping faucet or a running toilet is usually a fair DIY project. A parts store and twenty minutes will often solve it. But plumbing problems escalate quickly once water finds a path it should not be taking, and the line between "fixable this weekend" and "call someone now" is not always obvious.

children.text: 1. Water pressure drops suddenly

If you notice a gradual decrease in pressure over several months, it typically indicates mineral buildup. However, a sudden drop in pressure throughout your entire home suggests a more serious problem, such as a hidden leak, a malfunctioning pressure regulator, or a blockage in the main line. Simply tightening a fitting won't resolve these issues.
2. You smell sewage indoors

A blocked vent stack or a dried-out trap is usually the culprit behind unpleasant odors. This situation is not just bothersome; exposure to sewer gas poses health risks. Addressing the issue often requires a thorough diagnosis of the vent system rather than just focusing on the fixture closest to the smell.
3. Water heater is making noise

Popping or rumbling sounds usually mean sediment has built up at the bottom of the tank. Left alone, this reduces efficiency and can shorten the unit's life significantly. A flush is a simple fix — but repeated noise after a flush suggests the tank itself is failing.

If you hear popping or rumbling sounds, it usually means there’s sediment building up at the bottom of the tank. If you ignore it, it can hurt efficiency and even shorten the unit's lifespan. Flushing it out is an easy fix, but if the noise comes back after that, it might mean the tank is on its way out.
4. Multiple drains are slow at once

One slow drain is a local clog. Several slow drains at the same time usually means the problem is further down the line, in a section shared by multiple fixtures. Chemical drain cleaner will not reach it, and repeated dosing can damage older pipe.
"Before you decide to cut into a wall or a slab for repairs, it's wise to seek a second opinion. You might discover alternative solutions that could save you time and money."
5. You have already tried twice

If the same repair needs doing again within a few months, the underlying cause was never addressed. That is the clearest sign it is time for a proper diagnosis rather than a third attempt at the same patch.

If you find yourself needing the same repair again in just a few months, it’s a clear sign that the real issue wasn’t tackled. That’s when you know it’s time to get a proper diagnosis instead of just trying to patch it up again.
